shape: Radiocommunications licensing, Australia (ACMA low-interference-potential-devices class licence)
answer:
# LIPD class licence — digital modulation, 2400–2483.5 MHz (position as at 17 November 2026)

## 1. Answer

| Ask | Answer | Equivalent | Operative provision |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 — maximum EIRP for a digital modulation transmitter, 2400–2483.5 MHz | **4 W** | 4 000 mW = **36 dBm** EIRP | Schedule 1, table item 7 (Digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters, 2400–2483.5 MHz, Maximum EIRP 4 W) |
| 3 — additional limit on radiated peak power spectral density | **25 mW per 3 kHz** | 0.025 W / 3 kHz = **+13.98 dBm per 3 kHz** (≈ +14 dBm/3 kHz); −20.8 dBm/Hz | Clause 43 (additional limitation for table items 6, 7 and 9): the radiated peak power spectral density must not be greater than 25 mW per 3 kHz |
| 4 — year in the name of the instrument in force | **2025** | *Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025* | ACMA LIPD class licence page, licence rules section |

Both limits in rows 2 and 3 apply **cumulatively**. Compliance is assessed on **EIRP** (radiated), not conducted power plus a nominal antenna gain.

## 2. Which instrument is in force on 17 November 2026

The ACMA "Low interference potential devices (LIPD) class licence" page (fetched 2026-11-25T07:57:08Z, sha256 266c1d51ee88…, page last updated 02 October 2025) states, under *Licence rules*:

> "You don't need to apply for a class licence or pay any fees. But you must follow all the rules in the:
> Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025
> Radiocommunications Act 1992."

That page was captured eight days after the operative date and is ACMA's live statement of the governing instrument, so the instrument in force on 17 November 2026 is the **Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025**. The naming year, and therefore the answer to ask 4, is **2025**.

Two points follow directly:

- The project assumption that the instrument in force is the *Class Licence 2015* (as amended, with no renaming) is **not supported**. The strings "Low Interference Potential Devices Class Licence 2015", "Class Licence 2015" and "2015" do not occur anywhere in the 17 647-character full text of that page. The 2015 instrument has been replaced by the 2025 instrument, and any answer keyed to "2015" is keyed to a superseded instrument.
- No variation or replacement of the 2025 instrument between its commencement and 17 November 2026 is evidenced in the material retrieved; §7 sets out the one-minute documentary check that closes that residual gap.

## 3. The operative provisions

From Schedule 1 of the 2025 instrument (text as it appears in the March 2025 consultation draft, ACMA, sha256 8b43f35e37a6…):

> "7 Digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters | 2400–2483.5 MHz | 4 W | See clause 43"

> "43 Additional limitation for table items 6, 7 and 9
> A radiocommunications transmitter must not be operated if its radiated peak power spectral density is greater than 25 mW per 3 kHz."

Corroboration from the predecessor instrument — *Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2000*, compilation F2014C00930 prepared 14 July 2014, Schedule 1:

> "45A Digital modulation transmitters 2400–2483.5 4 W 1. The radiated peak power spectral density in any 3 kHz is limited to 25 mW per 3 kHz. 2. The minimum 6 dB bandwidth must be at least 500 kHz."

The 4 W / 25 mW-per-3 kHz pair is therefore stable across the 2000 and 2025 generations of the licence, which materially raises confidence in the figures for the 2025 instrument.

**Class boundary.** The same band carries separate frequency-hopping items (item 2: 500 mW with a minimum number of hopping frequencies under clause 40; item 3: 4 W with a larger minimum number of hopping frequencies under clause 41) and a separate 10 mW "any transmitter" entry. A device that hops must be assessed against the hopping item, not item 7; item 7 is the correct item for non-hopping digital modulation (DSSS/OFDM WLAN, proprietary wideband data links, etc.). Misclassification does not change the 4 W figure for item 3, but it does change the additional limitations that attach.

## 4. Conversions and internal consistency (arithmetic checked)

- 4 W → 10·log10(4000 mW) = **36.02 dBm** ≈ 36 dBm EIRP.
- 25 mW → 10·log10(25) = **13.98 dBm** per 3 kHz; expressed per hertz: 13.98 − 10·log10(3000) = **−20.79 dBm/Hz**; expressed in watts: **0.025 W per 3 kHz**.
- **Coherence check between the two limits.** For a flat-spectrum emission, EIRP and PSD are related by the emission width. The 4 W cap divided by the 25 mW-per-3 kHz cap gives a factor of 160, i.e. a minimum width of 160 × 3 kHz = **480 kHz** for a signal to sit at both caps simultaneously. At exactly 500 kHz width and 36 dBm EIRP, the average PSD is 36.0 − 10·log10(500/3) = 36.0 − 22.2 = **13.78 dBm/3 kHz**, which is below the 13.98 dBm/3 kHz cap — so the two limits are mutually consistent and neither is violated by the other. The historically attached "minimum 6 dB bandwidth 500 kHz" condition sits exactly at that boundary.
- **No figure in this deliverable exceeds a limit the same deliverable sets.** The PSD cap is not a restatement of the EIRP cap and cannot be satisfied by quoting total power: a 20 MHz-wide emission at the full 36 dBm has an average PSD of 36.0 − 10·log10(20000/3) = 36.0 − 38.2 = **−2.2 dBm/3 kHz**, comfortably inside the cap, whereas a narrowband emission can pass on PSD and fail on EIRP, or vice versa. Both must be tested.

## 5. Corrections to the assumptions carried in the project brief

1. **Year: 2015 → 2025.** See §2. The 2015 licence is not the instrument in force on 17 November 2026.
2. **PSD: "8 dBm in any 3 kHz measured in a 100 kHz bandwidth" is wrong for Australia.** 8 dBm/3 kHz is the United States FCC Part 15.247 figure. The Australian limit is 25 mW (13.98 dBm) per 3 kHz — 6 dB more permissive — and the Australian instrument states the limit directly as a radiated peak PSD in any 3 kHz; it does not import a 100 kHz measurement bandwidth, nor a "−2 dBW/3 kHz" formulation. Applying 8 dBm would understate the permitted PSD by 6 dB and could fail a compliant product at type-test.
3. **"Digital modulation" vs hopping.** The band is served by several table items; the 4 W figure attaches to item 7 (digital modulation) and item 3 (frequency hopping, with a hopping-frequencies condition). Confirm which item the device falls under before quoting 4 W.
4. **4 W is an EIRP cap, not a conducted-power cap.** Antenna gain counts in full.

## 6. On the harness proofs of absence

The proofs of absence are correct **as to the page they name and no other** — the ACMA LIPD landing page. That page is a plain-language consumer page: it explains what a class licence is, lists device types, points to the General Equipment Rules, the EMC Standard 2017 and the EME Standard, and warns about the Murchison Radioastronomy Observatory exclusion zone. It contains **no** occurrence of "maximum EIRP", "EIRP", "equivalent isotropically radiated power", "watts", "1 W" or "1 watt"; **no** occurrence of "radiated peak power spectral density", "peak power spectral density", "power spectral density", "PSD", "dBm/MHz" or "10 dBm/MHz"; and **no** occurrence of "2015". I have therefore not recorded asks 2 or 3 as "not stated": the figures are stated, in the 2025 licence text and in the predecessor compilation, both quoted in §3 — the silence is confined to the consumer page. Nor have I recorded ask 4 as "not stated": the absence of "2015" is precisely what establishes that the year carried in the name of the instrument now in force is **2025**, which the page states verbatim.

## 7. Documentary confirmation to run before certifying a product

The 4 W and 25 mW-per-3 kHz figures are read from the March 2025 consultation draft of the 2025 licence (the only 2025 text available in this session) and corroborated by the superseded 2000 compilation. The registered/made text was not retrieved here. Close that gap as follows, and file the result with the compliance record:

1. On the Federal Register of Legislation (legislation.gov.au), search the title *Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025*; open the compilation current as at 17 November 2026.
2. Record the FRLI number, the commencement date (must be on or before 17 November 2026) and the compilation date.
3. Confirm that no variation registered between the commencement date and 17 November 2026 alters the Schedule 1 table item for digital modulation in 2400–2483.5 MHz or the clause imposing the PSD limit.
4. Confirm the final item number (draft: item 7) and clause number (draft: clause 43) — numbering may shift between draft and made text.
5. Confirm whether a minimum 6 dB bandwidth condition (500 kHz in the 2000 item 45A) survives into the 2025 instrument. The draft clause 43 states only the PSD limit, which suggests the bandwidth condition was not carried forward; if it was dropped, the practical effect is that the 4 W EIRP cap becomes the binding constraint for wideband emissions, and narrowband emissions remain governed by the 3 kHz PSD cap.

## 8. Obligations adjacent to the EIRP limits (not limits themselves)

- Operation is also subject to the *Radiocommunications (Electromagnetic Compatibility) Standard 2017* and to the General Equipment Rules (general standards at Schedule 5; EME standard at Schedule 4) per the ACMA page.
- Devices within 70 km of the Murchison Radioastronomy Observatory (central Western Australia) are subject to additional place-based restrictions irrespective of EIRP.
- No interference protection is available under a class licence; the limits are conditions of the licence, not merely design targets.

## 9. Sources relied on

1. ACMA, *Low interference potential devices (LIPD) class licence*, https://www.acma.gov.au/licences/low-interference-potential-devices-lipd-class-licence — fetched 2026-11-25T07:57:08Z, sha256 266c1d51ee88…, page last updated 02 October 2025 (instrument identification; ask 4).
2. ACMA, *Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025* — draft for consultation, March 2025, https://www.acma.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-03/draft_radiocommunications_low_interference_potential_devices_class_licence_2025.pdf — fetched 2026-11-25T07:57:08Z, sha256 8b43f35e37a6… (Schedule 1 item 7; clause 43).
3. *Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2000*, compilation F2014C00930 prepared 14 July 2014, https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2005B00339/2014-07-08/text/original/pdf — fetched 2026-11-25T07:57:09Z, sha256 592c1cec4a54… (Schedule 1 item 45A; corroboration of 4 W and 25 mW per 3 kHz, and of the 500 kHz minimum 6 dB bandwidth).

question: X36
answer:
NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1 — Class R (EMI/RF) bond joint: what the standard actually requires

Short answer: NASA-STD-4003A does not state a maximum RF impedance in ohms at a stated frequency for a Class R bond joint. It states a qualitative RF requirement and one numeric joint limit, which is dc resistance, not RF impedance: 2.5 milliohms (0.0025 ohm) maximum dc resistance across each joint in the Class R path.

1. The Class R clause (NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1, 4.1.4; original 4003A 4.1.4 has the same technical content without EBR numbers):
- 4.1.4: 'The intent of Class R bonding is to provide a uniform low impedance path for all electrical equipment at radio frequencies. Refer to Appendix B.3.4 for more information.'
- 4.1.4.a [EBR 20]: 'All electrical and electronic equipment shall be bonded using the methods described in section 5.1 to provide a low impedance path from the equipment enclosure to structure.'
- 4.1.4.b [EBR 21]: 'All Class R bond paths to structure, and the joints in that path, shall be designed such that the inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest.'
- 4.1.4.b(1) [EBR 22]: 'The direct current (dc) resistance across each joint in the path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms.'
- 4.1.4.c [EBR 23]: 'The design and construction of the outer mold line of the vehicle shall implement Class R electrical bonding between all outer mold line components so as to inherently provide a uniform low impedance enclosure surrounding the vehicle.'

2. The bonding-class table describes Class R as: 'Requires low RF impedance at high frequency. Direct contact preferred. No jumpers. Short, wide strap may be used as last resort.' Its DC bond resistance entry for Class R is: 'Bonding resistance requirement, 2.5 milliohms or less. Low inductance required.' Its frequency requirement is 'High' and current requirement 'Low'. 'High' is not a stated frequency; no numeric band is given.

3. The standard's own Appendix B.3.4 rationale is explicit that 2.5 milliohms is not an RF design limit:
- 'There is no RF design basis for the historical 2.5-milliohm requirement except to ensure a good metal-to-metal contact that can be expected to be consistent. The basic requirement is to have low impedance at the frequency or frequencies of interest. The value of this impedance depends upon the quality of the surface preparation...'
- 'The 2.5-milliohm dc resistance requirement is good for a standard, but one should not assume a good RF bond exists just because the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms. Also, extra effort need not be made just to satisfy the dc requirement if the RF impedance is much higher due to the inductance of the configuration. Look at the whole configuration to get the lowest impedance possible at the frequencies of interest to produce a good RF bond.'
- The appendix also explains that the total impedance is resistive at low frequency, rises inductively with frequency, and at parallel resonance may rise sharply depending on the ratio of reactance to resistance (Q); hence the standard requires the design to consider resonances across the frequencies of interest rather than meet one ohms-at-frequency number.

Therefore the three asks resolve as follows:
- Ask 1 (maximum RF impedance value): NOT_STATED. NASA-STD-4003A states no numeric maximum RF impedance in ohms at a stated frequency. Do not report 2.5 milliohms as an RF impedance; it is dc resistance.
- Ask 2 (in ohms at a stated frequency): NO_STATED_FREQUENCY. The standard does not define the 'frequencies of interest' and gives no ohms-at-frequency limit. The program must define the frequency band(s).
- Ask 3 (what the standard actually requires for a Class R joint): QUALITATIVE_LOW_IMPEDANCE_PLUS_DC_2.5_MILLIOHMS. The joint must provide a low-impedance path at the frequencies of interest with low inductance and no harmful resonances; direct contact is preferred, no jumpers, a short wide strap is a last resort; and dc resistance across each joint must be <= 2.5 milliohms (0.0025 ohm).

What to do for the design (since the standard does not supply the RF number):
1. Confirm the contractually applicable revision. The current public document is NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1 (original 2013-02-05; revalidated 03-13-2026). The original 4003A and Change 1 have the same Class R technical requirement in the quoted clauses; Change 1 adds EBR numbers and cites Appendix B.3.4 instead of A.3.4. Check for program tailoring or a tighter program EMC spec. The NASA standards page lists the document as not a NASA mandatory standard, so program applicability and tailoring must be confirmed.
2. Obtain the program's frequencies of interest (emitter/receiver bands, CE/RE test bands, antenna and cable shield frequencies) and any EMC margin requirement. NASA-STD-4003A does not define them.
3. Derive a project-specific maximum bond transfer impedance Z_max(f) from the EMC/EMI budget (allowed voltage across the joint for a given current, or allowed shield termination impedance) and put it in the bond control plan as a tailored requirement. Format it as: Z_bond(f) <= Z_max(f) for f in [f1, f2], plus dc resistance <= 2.5 milliohms per joint. Do not label Z_max(f) as a NASA-STD-4003A number; it is a program-tailored value.
4. Design the joint for direct metal-to-metal contact, short/wide/low-inductance geometry, no jumpers, surface preparation per section 5.1, and avoidance of series/parallel resonances in the band. The 2.5 milliohm dc limit is a screen, not the RF design criterion.
5. Verify dc resistance across each joint with a four-wire Kelvin micro-ohmmeter; verify RF impedance/transfer impedance at the program-defined frequencies with a program-approved method (network analyzer/current probe or equivalent), and inspect for direct contact and no jumpers. Record the method and frequencies in the verification plan.
6. If a supplier or reviewer quotes 'Class R max RF impedance = 2.5 milliohms,' correct it: that is the dc resistance limit from 4.1.4.b(1). The NTRS connector salt-spray paper's '<2.5 mΩ' Class R check is also a dc bonding measurement, not an RF impedance requirement.

Applicability note: Appendix B.3.4 notes that the Class R bond is not required on all equipment, but it is difficult to determine in advance which equipment really needs it; low impedance to structure is necessary for certain power-line-to-equipment chassis filters and for proper operation of cable shields terminated to equipment chassis. Resolve applicability in the program's bond control plan rather than assuming every joint is Class R or that none is.

Traceability: NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1, 4.1.4 and Appendix B.3.4; original NASA-STD-4003A, 4.1.4 and Appendix A.3.4. The harness's full-text word-search proof of absence for ask 1 found none of 'RF impedance', 'impedance', or 'ohms' in the NASA standards metadata page, standards-csv/239, and NTRS 20140008725; the standard's own Class R text quoted above is the direct source showing no numeric RF impedance limit.
cautions: The answer says ask 1 is not stated in the document. The only check behind that is a search of the pages read in full for the words a model listed as the ones such an answer would be printed with, and it found none. The largest page searched for it had 33,901 characters.

answer:
# MUTCD 11th Edition, Section 4I.06 — Pedestrian Intervals and Signal Phases
## Answers to the three questions, with citations and application notes

### 0. Sources used and evidence standard

All answers below are read from the FHWA-published 11th Edition text (December 2023, including Revision 1 dated December 2025), Section 4I.06, which begins on page 722:

| Source | Identifier in the evidence set | What it establishes |
|---|---|---|
| FHWA MUTCD 11th Ed., Part 4 (part4r1.pdf) | sha256 bd427184b2f0 | Primary text of §4I.06, ¶04 and the pedestrian-clearance-time guidance |
| FHWA MUTCD 11th Ed. – Revision 1, Dec 2025 (part4r1.pdf, p.724) | sha256 bd427184b2f0 | Confirms the 2 s buffer and 3.5 ft/s survive Rev 1 unchanged |
| Indiana IMUTCD, Part 4, 11th Ed. | sha256 420b95b73d05 | Independent reproduction of the same ¶04 language |
| Caltrans CAMUTCD 2026 draft, Ch. 4I | sha256 877d6d2a49db | Reproduces FHWA 2023 ¶04 and the 3.5 ft/s clearance-time sentence verbatim |
| MUTCD 11th Ed. cover + table of contents | sha256 7aad55eacf4f | Section location only (§4I.06, p.722) — no substantive text |

Terminology used throughout, per the request: **buffer interval** = the steady UPRAISED HAND (DONT WALK) indication that follows the flashing UPRAISED HAND **pedestrian change interval**, before any conflicting vehicular movement is released.

---

### 1. Ask 1 — Minimum buffer interval: **2 seconds**

Section 4I.06, Paragraph 4 (Standard), page 722, verbatim:

> "Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 2 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement. The sum of the time of the pedestrian change interval and the buffer interval shall not be less than the calculated pedestrian clearance time (see Paragraphs 7 through 16 of this Section). The buffer interval shall not begin later than the beginning of the red clearance interval, if used."

**Value: 2 seconds.** This is a *Standard* ("shall"), not Guidance — it is an enforceable floor, and a timing plan that releases conflicting traffic on the falling edge of the flashing UPRAISED HAND is non-compliant regardless of how much pedestrian clearance time was provided. The requirement is reproduced identically in Revision 1 (p.724), in the Indiana IMUTCD, and in the Caltrans 2026 draft, so there is no edition-drift risk within the 11th Edition.

Three companion constraints sit in the same paragraph and must be enforced together in the controller, not traded against each other:

1. **Sum rule.** `pedestrian change interval + buffer interval ≥ calculated pedestrian clearance time (PCT)`. The buffer is *part of* the pedestrian clearance time budget; it is not an add-on. Figure 4I-4, note ***, states it directly: "The Buffer Interval, which shall always be provided and displayed, may be used to help satisfy the calculated pedestrian clearance time, or may begin after the calculated pedestrian clearance time has ended."
2. **Start constraint.** The buffer shall not begin later than the beginning of the red clearance interval, if a red clearance interval is used.
3. **Always provided.** Figure 4I-4, note ***: the buffer "shall always be provided and displayed" — it cannot be dropped because the countdown reached zero early or because the vehicular phase needs the green.

Related, but a different provision — Section 4I.04, Paragraph 7 (Guidance), for a pedestrian signal head with **no concurrent vehicular phase**: the pedestrian change interval "should be set to be approximately 4 seconds less than the required pedestrian clearance time (see Section 4I.06) and an additional clearance interval (during which a steady UPRAISED HAND is displayed) should be provided prior to the start of the conflicting vehicular phase." That additional steady interval is the buffer in a non-concurrent application; the 2 s floor of ¶04 still governs.

Also note Section 4I.04, ¶06: countdown displays shall not be used during the red clearance interval of a concurrent vehicular phase that ends simultaneously with or after the end of the pedestrian phase. The buffer, by contrast, may overlap the yellow change and red clearance intervals — Figure 4I-4 explicitly shows four permitted relationships in which the buffer equals all or part of the yellow change + red clearance intervals.

### 2. Ask 2 — Default walking speed for pedestrian clearance time: **3.5 feet per second**

Section 4I.06, pedestrian clearance time guidance, verbatim:

> "The pedestrian clearance time should be sufficient to allow a pedestrian crossing in the crosswalk who left the curb or edge of pavement at the end of the WALKING PERSON (symbolizing WALK) signal indication to travel at a walking speed of 3.5 feet per second to at least the far side of the traveled way or to a median of sufficient width for pedestrians to wait."

and, immediately following, Paragraph 10:

> "Where pedestrians who walk slower than 3.5 feet per second, or pedestrians who use wheelchairs, routinely use the crosswalk, a walking speed of less than 3.5 feet per second should be considered in determining the pedestrian clearance time."

**Value: 3.5 ft/s (1.07 m/s).** Points to hold onto when applying it:

- It is a *Guidance* ("should"), not a Standard, so a documented engineering study can justify a lower value — but 3.5 ft/s is the default that applies **absent** such a study, and it is the value an auditor will check against.
- 3.5 ft/s applies to the **pedestrian clearance time** (flashing UPRAISED HAND + buffer). It does **not** apply to the walk interval. The walk interval is separately governed: "the walk interval should be at least 7 seconds in length so that pedestrians will have adequate opportunity to leave the curb or shoulder before the pedestrian clearance time begins" (Guidance, ¶11), with walk intervals as short as 4 seconds permitted where volumes and characteristics do not require 7 seconds (Option, ¶12). Do not back-calculate the walk interval from the crossing distance.
- The measured distance is curb (or shoulder) to the far side of the traveled way, or to a median of sufficient width to wait — not curb to curb of the full roadway where a usable refuge exists.
- Because 3.5 ft/s is slower than the value used in older editions, any timing plan carried over from a pre-2023 design should be re-run rather than re-labeled; the clearance time will increase for the same crossing distance.

### 3. Worked timing calculations (showing the two answers do not conflict)

Procedure: (a) PCT = crossing distance ÷ walking speed, rounded up to the next whole second; (b) buffer = 2 s minimum; (c) pedestrian change interval (flashing) = PCT − buffer, rounded up; (d) verify pedestrian change interval + buffer ≥ PCT and buffer ≥ 2 s; (e) release conflicting vehicular movement only at the end of the buffer.

| Case | Crossing distance | Speed used | PCT = d/v | Buffer | Flashing UPRAISED HAND | Sum (flashing + buffer) | Check |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A — default | 60 ft | 3.5 ft/s | 17.14 → 18 s | 2 s | 16 s | 18 s | 18 ≥ 17.14 ✓, buffer 2 s ✓ |
| B — slow-pedestrian population | 60 ft | 3.0 ft/s (justified per ¶10) | 20.00 → 20 s | 2 s | 18 s | 20 s | 20 ≥ 20.00 ✓ (equal, permitted — rule is "not less than"), buffer 2 s ✓ |
| C — narrow crossing | 24 ft | 3.5 ft/s | 6.86 → 7 s | 2 s | 5 s | 7 s | 7 ≥ 6.86 ✓, buffer 2 s ✓; countdown optional here (Figure 4I-4 note *: optional for pedestrian change intervals of 7 s or less) |

Full phase for Case A: WALK 7 s → flashing UPRAISED HAND 16 s → steady UPRAISED HAND 2 s → conflicting green released. If a red clearance interval is used on the conflicting approach, the buffer may run concurrently with it, but the buffer must not begin later than the beginning of that red clearance interval, and the conflicting green still cannot start until the buffer has fully elapsed.
